title: Nanak on the mountain
hookLine: Bhai Gurdas tells of the yogis on Mount Sumer asking Nanak about the world below (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)

lines: SO, HOW ARE THINGS DOWN THERE?
cards: So, how are things down there? It's what you ask someone who's just come in from outside. In Bhai Gurdas's first var, it's asked on a mountain.
Guru Nanak climbs up to Sumer, and the siddhs are there, yogis who have left the world far below them to practice in the heights. They see him arrive, and they ask him for news.
Year one told what Nanak said to yogis about living in the world. Today, Bhai Gurdas's version of the question, and the answer he remembers. Today: siddhs.

teach.h: WHAT'S HAPPENING IN THE WORLD BELOW?
teach.b: In Bhai Gurdas's telling, the siddhs ask Nanak what's happening in the world of mortals, the world below. A polite question, maybe a curious one. Nanak's answer is not small talk.
He says truth has become like a moon that can't be seen, and falsehood like a moonless dark. He says he has gone out searching through that dark. Then he turns the question around.
The siddhs, he says, have gone and hidden in the mountains.

teach.h: WHO WILL CARRY THE WORLD ACROSS?
teach.b: So who is going to carry the world across? There's an edge to that. The yogis asked about the world below as if it were somebody else's problem, interesting news from far away.

Nanak answers as if they're part of the story: the people best trained in stillness and discipline have climbed out of reach, just when the world needs them. Bhai Gurdas is not mocking the siddhs' discipline.
He takes it seriously, which is why the question bites. Training means something because of what it's for. Holiness, in this telling, doesn't belong up on the mountain looking down.

teach.h: THE WORK IS IN THE VALLEY.
teach.b: It belongs back in the valley, with the farmers, the traders, the families, the people living in the dark. Which is where Nanak himself is going: tomorrow to Mecca, and soon, home to Kartarpur.
The mountain is a place to visit.
The world below is where the work is.

how: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's meetings with the siddhs, told by Bhai Gurdas and in the Siddh Gosht of the Guru Granth Sahib, as a call to live a holy life within the world rather than withdrawing from it.

o: Sikh elders who welcomed Nanak to the mountain
yogis who left the world below for the heights
pilgrims climbing to a temple on the summit

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: asked for news of the world below
like a moon that can't be seen
asked who would carry the world across

s: in Bhai Gurdas's telling, Nanak praises the siddhs for leaving the world
he asks who will carry the world across while they hide in the mountains.
the siddhs ask Nanak what is happening in the world below
it's their question, and he turns it back on them.

games.q: you're Nanak, standing among yogis high on the mountain. they ask, kindly, for news of the world below. what do you say?
o: all is well; stay where you are.
it's dark down there, and you've gone to hide. who will carry it across?
nothing, and stay up here with them.
games.why: in Bhai Gurdas's telling, Nanak says truth is hidden like the moon, and asks who will carry the world across while the siddhs hide in the mountains.

practice: Stand somewhere a little high, the top of a staircase, an upstairs window, even the step outside your door, and look down at the street and the people passing.
Ask the siddhs' question honestly, what is happening down there, who is struggling, and let one face or one place come to mind. If you pray, you can hold that person in the Name for a while.

wordCard.voice: Siddhs, yogis who climbed Sumer to leave the world below, asking Nanak for its news, and hearing him ask back who would carry that world across.

carryVoice: Your line: what of the world below. Nanak's answer was to go back down. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, pauris 28–29 (Nanak on Sumer; the siddhs' question)
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 938 (Ramkali, Siddh Gosht, opening)
